title: The archer who dropped his bow
hookLine: Arjuna lets his bow fall in grief at Kurukshetra, and Krishna calls yoga evenness, skill in action, the unjoining from sorrow
tomorrow: caged parrots argue about the Veda at a front door. whose house is it?

cards: Two armies face each other at Kurukshetra, and the conch shells blow. Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, asks his charioteer to drive into the open ground between them, so he can see who he's about to fight.
And he sees his teachers. His grandfather. His cousins and his friends.
His limbs go weak, his mouth goes dry, his skin burns. I won't fight, he says. His great bow slips from his hand, and he sinks down in the chariot, overcome with grief.
His charioteer is Krishna. What Krishna says next is the Bhagavad Gita.

teach.b: And the word Krishna reaches for again and again is yoga. Not a pose. In the Gita, yoga is first evenness: do your work standing the same in success and failure, Krishna says; that evenness is called yoga.
Two verses later: yoga is skill in action.

And in the sixth chapter, a line with a twist: yoga is the unjoining from sorrow, cutting the tie between a person and their pain. Notice what Krishna does with a weeping friend. He doesn't send him home.
He teaches him who he really is: the self in every being, the atman, is not killed when the body is killed. Then he teaches him how to act while the heart is heavy.
This is karma yoga, the yoga of action: do what's yours to do, as an offering, without clutching at how it turns out.
The Gita also speaks of a yoga of knowledge and a yoga of devotion, and Hindu tradition keeps them all.
Patanjali's school is one careful version, where posture, asana, is one limb of eight: a seat steady and comfortable enough to look inward. So which is the real yoga? Hindus have never had to choose.
But on a hard day, the Gita's meaning is the one close at hand. Many teachers read it this way: yoga isn't feeling nothing.

teach.h: YOU CAN STILL DO YOUR PART.
teach.b: It's not being ruled by the sorrow, so you can still do your part.

how: Many Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna teaches the grieving Arjuna the yogas of action, knowledge and devotion; in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, posture is one limb among eight, a steady and comfortable seat.

o: evenness, skill in action, the unjoining from sorrow
a set of poses Krishna lists one by one
a word Krishna uses only once, for sitting still

games.q: the faces of yoga — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna sends the grieving Arjuna home from the battle
he stays with him and teaches him: the self is not killed, and how to act with evenness.
in the Gita, Krishna calls evenness of mind yoga
standing the same in success and failure, he says, is called yoga.
in Patanjali, posture is the whole of yoga
asana is one limb among eight, a steady, comfortable seat for looking inward.

games.q: your friend has to speak at her grandfather's memorial and is scared she'll cry. in the Gita's yoga, what's the aim?
o: feel nothing, so she won't cry
evenness: not ruled by the sorrow, so she can still do her part
skip it; grief means it isn't hers to do
games.why: evenness. Arjuna dropped his bow in grief, and Krishna taught him yoga so he could act. many teachers read 'unjoining from sorrow' as not being ruled by it, not as feeling nothing.

practice: Sit the way Patanjali describes: steady, not rigid, comfortable, not slumped. Bring to mind one thing that's yours to do this week that feels heavy.
Hold it without pushing the feeling away, and let the breath stay even underneath it. If you pray, offer the task to Krishna, or to whatever you pray to, before you begin.
If you don't, say quietly: i'll do my part, and let go of how it turns out.

wordCard.voice: Yoga. In the Gita, evenness of mind, skill in action, and the unjoining from sorrow. In Patanjali, a steady and comfortable seat on the way to stillness.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a seat or posture; in Patanjali, one of the eight limbs, steady and comfortable.

carryVoice: Your line: yoga, evenness, even in sorrow. Arjuna wept, and still picked up the bow. I'll be here tomorrow.
